The `hpc` subcommand is used to configure HPC environments.

## Commands

```
  hpc       Master HPC setup
  hpc scratch [--r]
  hpc apptainer
  hpc slurm
  hpc login git
  hpc git
  hpc r
```

## Installation

Assuming that the HPC is running on Linux, the following line will install `setupmjr` without requiring `sudo` permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MiguelRodo/setupmjr/main/install-local.sh | bash
```

Confirm that installation worked by running:

```bash
setupmjr --version
```

If the above does not work, then `setupmjr` may not be on your system `PATH`. In that case, you can add the following line to your shell profile (typically `~/.bashrc`):

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Then run:

```
source ~/.bashrc`.
```

At this point, the following should succeed:

```bash
setupmjr --version
```

If not, then the initial installation failed.

## Setup

The following command will configure the HPC environment:

```bash
setupmjr hpc
```

Apart from needing to edit one file for Git authentication if this has not been setup yet (see below), this command requires no other user input.

`setupmjr hpc` does the following:

- *Helps store large files effectively*: Large files are stored in the `/scratch` space (if available) rather than `/home`, to respect HPC storage policies.
- *Authenticates with Git*: Scripts are added to which the user needs to simply add their GitHub username and a personal access token (PAT) to enable seamless Git operations from the HPC environment.
- *Add `Apptainer` and `SLURM` helpers*: If these tools are available on the HPC, helper scripts will be added to simplify their usage.

Each of these features can be configured independently via the respective subcommands (`hpc scratch`, `hpc apptainer`, `hpc slurm`, `hpc git`, `hpc r`).

### Setting up Git

To work with Git, you need to do two things:

1. Supply Git with your name and email (if not already configured).
2. Provide Git with credentials to authenticate with remote repositories, e.g. GitHub.

To set this up, run the following command (which is also part of the `setupmjr hpc` command):

```bash
setupmjr hpc git
```

You will be prompted to enter your full name and email address (if these are not already set), which Git uses to identify you as the author of commits.

In addition, you will be prompted to enter your GitHub username and a personal access token (PAT). This allows Git to authenticate with GitHub when you push commits or perform other operations that require authentication.

To get a GitHUB PAT, go to your GitHub account settings, navigate to "Developer settings" > "Personal access tokens", and generate a new token with the appropriate scopes (e.g. `repo` for full control of private repositories).

If you skip entering any of the above information, you can always run `setupmjr hpc git` again to set it up later.

::: {.callout-info collapse="true"}
## Details

Git authentication is configured by the following:

1. It is ensured that `.bashrc.d` files are sourced by `.bashrc`.

2. The credential helper is set to the following:

    ```
    !f() { sleep 1; echo "username=${GITHUB_USER:-TOKEN}"; echo "password=${GH_TOKEN:-$GITHUB_TOKEN}"; }; f
    ```
3. A script is added to `~/.bashrc.d/login.sh`, which has space for the user to add their GitHub username and PAT, and then exports these as environment variables (`GITHUB_USER` and `GITHUB_USERNAME` for the user name and `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_PAT` for the token). 
:::

### Using scratch space

HPCs typically have a separate scratch space for storing large files (i.e. `/scratch/$USER`), which is often faster and has different quotas than the home directory.
The `setupmjr hpc scratch` command helps you configure your environment to use this scratch space effectively.

To set this up, run the following command (also part of `setupmjr hpc`):

```bash
setupmjr hpc scratch
```

This configures your environment to preferentially use the `/scratch` space for the following:

- Apptainer and Singularity images
  - Automatically cached in `/scratch/$USER/.cache/<apptainer/singularity>` instead of the default location in the home directory.
- R libraries:
  - The `R_LIBS_USER` environment variable is set to `/scratch/$USER/.local/lib/R` and created, so that R packages are installed in the scratch space instead of the home directory.
  - Similarly, various `RENV_*` environment variables configuring `renv` paths are set to point to the scratch space.


### `hpc slurm`

The `hpc slurm` command sets up several utility scripts for interacting with the Slurm workload manager, placing them in `~/.local/bin`:

- `slurm-sbatch`: Submits a Slurm job using `sbatch` and logs the submission details, including the submitted script contents and standard output, into a specified or default log directory (`_tmp/log/sbatch`).
- `slurm-sintx`: Starts an interactive Slurm session using `sintx`. By default, it requests 2 tasks (`--ntasks=2`) and 1 node (`--nodes=1`). You can specify the number of tasks as the first argument, and pass additional flags to `sintx` thereafter (e.g., `slurm-sintx 4 --mem=10G`).
- `slurm-squeue`: Lists the current jobs for the logged-in user using `squeue -u $USER`. You can pass additional flags to `squeue` by providing them as arguments (e.g., `slurm-squeue --format="%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"`).

### `hpc r`

On an HPC, one may often use a non-standard `R` terminal named `radian` because it is better than the standard `R` terminal and the `RStudio` terminal is not available.
However, `radian` (in my experience) breaks without a key configuration setting.

To configure this setting, run the following command (which is also part of `setupmjr hpc`):

```bash
setupmjr hpc r
```

In addition to the above, object length and line linters are turned off (to prevent VS Code bothering you because your variable names or lines are "too long").

::::{.callout-info collapse="true"}
## Details

The `~/.radian_profile` file is created if it does not exist, and the following line is added to it:

```bash
options(radian.auto_match = FALSE)
```

The `~/.lintr` file is also created if it does not exist, and the following lines are added to it:

```bash
linters: linters_with_defaults(
    object_length_linter = NULL,
    object_name_linter = NULL)
```
::::
